{"id": "79:46/q06", "question": "What does ḍuḥā mean in this phrase?", "turns_on": "Whether ḍuḥā names a bounded morning period, extends to the whole day, or symbolizes worldly life; Bint al-Shati appeals to other Quranic uses.", "positions": [{"id": "79:46/q06/p1", "position": "The day's bright morning or forenoon, from sunrise until noon in explicit definitions.", "reasons": "Muqatil says morning until the sun rises higher; Ibn Abbas as transmitted by Ibn Kathir and Bursevi define sunrise to noon. Bint al-Shati cites Quranic uses opposite evening, the bringing forth of sunlight at 79:29, and appointed event time at 7:98 and 20:59; these oppose taking it as the whole day. Al-Damghani defines ḍuḥā as the sunlit beginning of the day, opposed here to evening. Ibn al-Jawzi derives it from visibility and the spread of sunlight, adducing ordinary uses for open exposure, sacrifice at forenoon, bright nights, and prominent outskirts; he and reported exegetes identify 79:46 as a forenoon use, also citing 20:59 and 93:1."}, {"id": "79:46/q06/p2", "position": "The early or dawn side of the day.", "reasons": "Al-Wahidi al-Wajiz and al-Baghawi describe the early morning or dawn; Ibn al-Jawzi calls it the first part. Al-Farra's Arabic pairing makes it the beginning opposed to evening's end."}, {"id": "79:46/q06/p3", "position": "It can stand metaphorically for the whole day.", "reasons": "Al-Tibi, reported by Alusi, allows evening or forenoon to stand for the day; the added pronoun reinforces it, like saying one saw with one's own eyes. Alusi allows the pronoun to reinforce this reading too. Bint al-Shati weighs against it from Quranic usage. Al-Zarkashi says the short forenoon can stand for the whole day."}, {"id": "79:46/q06/p4", "position": "The morning represents worldly life when people see the Hereafter.", "reasons": "Study Quran reports this from some commentators and mentions 93:1."}]}
{"id": "79:46/q07", "question": "How does 'or its forenoon' attach the morning to the evening?", "turns_on": "Whether the suffix has a same-day antecedent, licenses an adjacent morning, is merely additive, or reinforces a whole-day metaphor; the Quranic phrasing and Arabic idiom are invoked.", "positions": [{"id": "79:46/q07/p1", "position": "The suffix refers to the evening by an expansive attachment: its forenoon is the morning of the same day.", "reasons": "Al-Zajjaj and Ibn al-Jawzi identify the final alif and ha as referring to ʿashiyyah; al-Tabrisi, al-Razi's grammarians, al-Qurtubi, al-Nasafi and others license the attachment because both periods belong to one day, though morning ordinarily precedes evening. Al-Samin calls it figurative and notes the cadence. Al-Farra's example from a Banu Uqayl poet uses ʿashiyyat al-hilal for the new moon's setting or hidden phase; al-Thaʿlabi, Ibn al-Jawzi and al-Qurtubi repeat it. Ibn Atiyya cites brevity; Abu Hayyan calls the idafa expansive. Ibn ʿAbd al-Salam, as reported by al-Zarkashi, says relating the forenoon to the evening's day makes the spans comparable: a long day's forenoon could otherwise equal a short day's evening."}, {"id": "79:46/q07/p2", "position": "The expression can pair an evening with its following morning, as Arabic pairs the ends of adjacent periods.", "reasons": "Al-Farra allows an evening with the next morning or a morning with its previous evening. Al-Zajjaj distinguishes 'morning and its evening' of the same day from 'evening and its morning' of the following day. Al-Wahidi and al-Razi report al-Farra and al-Zajjaj's day association while also citing the next-morning idiom; Ibn al-Jawzi transmits al-Farra's paired-end explanation. Al-Kashshaf as reported by Alusi says the possessive wording rules out a stretch from one day's evening to another day's forenoon."}, {"id": "79:46/q07/p3", "position": "The final alif and ha are grammatical additions, so the sense is simply 'an evening or a morning'.", "reasons": "Ata from Ibn Abbas, reported by al-Wahidi al-Basit and al-Razi, treats the ending as additive rather than a time relation."}, {"id": "79:46/q07/p4", "position": "The suffix reinforces a metaphor in which either end stands for the entire day.", "reasons": "Al-Tibi, reported by Alusi, compares the emphasis to 'I saw with my own eyes.' Alusi allows this reinforcement, though he prefers the less forced ordinary attachment."}, {"id": "79:46/q07/p5", "position": "The suffix refers to the day implied by the evening, since an evening itself has no morning.", "reasons": "Al-Suyuti explicitly assigns the pronoun to the implied day. Al-Zarkashi also identifies it as that same day's forenoon."}]}
{"id": "79:46/q08", "question": "Why is their past stay perceived as so brief?", "turns_on": "The notes variously ground the perceived compression in encounter with the Hereafter, terror, ordinary perception of the past, or the nature of earthly time.", "positions": [{"id": "79:46/q08/p1", "position": "Seeing the Hereafter or Resurrection makes worldly duration shrink in retrospect.", "reasons": "Qatada's formulation appears through Abd al-Razzaq, al-Tabari, al-Tabrisi, Ibn Kathir and al-Suyuti. Al-Nasafi and Jishumi stress the Resurrection's overwhelming condition and terrors. Qushayri attributes the apparent brevity of the stay beneath the earth to the terror of seeing the Resurrection. {"id": "79:46/q09", "question": "What lesson does the brief comparison convey?", "turns_on": "The authors draw different lessons from the same perceived brevity: worldly transience, imminent judgment, or the gravity of Resurrection.", "positions": [{"id": "79:46/q09/p1", "position": "Worldly pleasures and life pass quickly, so the warning calls for preparation.", "reasons": "Al-Nahhas warns that worldly people soon leave pleasures. {"id": "79:46/q10", "question": "How does this comparison relate to other Quranic statements about time at judgment?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "79:46/q10/p1", "position": "It echoes statements that people will reckon their past as an hour, a day, or part of one.", "reasons": "Al-Mawardi and al-Qurtubi cite 10:45; al-Wahidi al-Basit, al-Baghawi, al-Kashshaf, al-Razi, al-Baydawi and al-Nasafi invoke 46:35. {"id": "79:46/q11", "question": "How does this closing comparison answer the earlier question about the Hour?", "turns_on": "Whether the preceding question is treated as a request for its unknown date, an impatient taunt, or a warning whose fulfillment will seem near; the reports differ on asking versus mentioning it.", "positions": [{"id": "79:46/q11/p1", "position": "It confirms the warning: the Hour will arrive swiftly and the Prophet's task is warning, while God knows its time.", "reasons": "Alusi prefers a short stay after the warning or threat and says the sentence may be circumstantial or independent. {"id": "83:1/q04", "question": "Why are they called mutaffifīn?", "turns_on": "Whether the term is explained by the smallness of the missing amount, the brim of a nearly full measure, stealth, or another proposed root.", "positions": [{"id": "83:1/q04/p1", "position": "The name points to the tiny amount removed or withheld.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī, al-Zajjāj, Abū Isḥāq and others derive it from ṭafīf, a slight thing. Biqāʿī cites the saying that Adam's children are only a slight measure apart."}, {"id": "83:1/q04/p2", "position": "It comes from ṭaff or ṭafāf, the edge or nearly full rim of a measure.", "reasons": "Al-Zajjāj and others derive it from the edge; al-Thaʿlabī cites ṭifāf for an almost-full vessel and ka-ṭaff al-ṣāʿ for a vessel left short. {"id": "83:1/q05", "question": "What event occasioned this warning?", "turns_on": "Which report supplies the immediate setting and whether the reported Anṣār setting fits the surah's provenance and its moral argument.", "positions": [{"id": "83:1/q05/p1", "position": "Medinan traders' dishonest measuring prompted the warning when the Prophet arrived, and they then improved.", "reasons": "Muqātil says the Prophet warned traders and God confirmed him by revelation. Islāhī reports the Anṣār version but objects that Meccan traders were at least as plausible and the surah was Meccan. Ibn ʿAbbās reports that the Prophet found Medina's people especially dishonest in measuring on arrival and that their measures improved after revelation; al-Suyūṭī calls this report's chain sound."}, {"id": "83:1/q05/p2", "position": "The warning addressed Abū Juhayna, who used separate measures for buying and selling.", "reasons": "Al-Suddī names him; Abū Hurayra calls him his uncle, and al-Qurṭubī also gives the name ʿAmr. {"id": "83:1/q06", "question": "Where and when was this surah or its opening revealed?", "turns_on": "Conflicting Meccan, Medinan, and mixed reports, plus whether the early Medinan trade occasion applies to the entire surah or only its opening.", "positions": [{"id": "83:1/q06/p1", "position": "It was revealed in Medina, especially at the Prophet's arrival; some call it the first revelation there.", "reasons": "Al-Ḥasan and al-Ḍaḥḥāk place it in Medina; al-Farrāʾ and Ibn ʿAbbās place its warning at arrival. One Ibn ʿAbbās report calls it the first surah revealed there; Abū Ḥayyān records the same claim. The Medinan measurement reports support an early Medinan opening. Al-Zarkashī attributes Medinan dating to Ibn ʿAbbās. Ibn al-Ghars cites Medina's prevalence of measure fraud for that dating. Ibn ʿAbbās's report places the warning after the Prophet's arrival; al-Suyūṭī grades its chain sound."}, {"id": "83:1/q06/p2", "position": "It was revealed in Mecca, perhaps the last revelation there.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAbbās, Ibn al-Zubayr, Ibn Masʿūd, al-Ḍaḥḥāk and Muqātil are cited for Meccan origin, though other reports from Ibn ʿAbbās and Muqātil differ. Mujāhid calls this the last Meccan revelation, against other proposed last surahs, al-ʿAnkabūt and al-Muʾminūn. Al-Burhān says reliable transmitters establish the ordering and counts 85 Meccan surahs. Al-Suyūṭī, as cited by Asad, is among authorities calling it last Meccan; Islāhī treats the surah as Meccan. Al-Zarkashī reports ʿAṭāʾ calling it the last surah revealed in Mecca. Ibn al-Ghars records the mention of ancient fables as an argument for Meccan dating."}, {"id": "83:1/q06/p3", "position": "Its parts span Mecca and Medina, or it was revealed between the cities.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAbbās and Qatāda reportedly say it is Medinan except the final eight Meccan verses. One account places the first four after arrival and verses 5–28 in Medina, with the final eight among the last in Mecca. Asad weighs the main body as late Meccan and the opening as early Medinan, a threshold like surah 29; another account places revelation between the cities before arrival. Ibn al-Ghars records both a Meccan dating except for the fraud account and a revelation between Mecca and Medina."}]}
{"id": "83:1/q07", "question": "What consequences and moral warnings does the verse support?", "turns_on": "How the warning is applied: direct afterlife threat, communal calamity, the gravity of slight fraud, duties of fair exchange, and illustrative reports.", "positions": [{"id": "83:1/q07/p1", "position": "Fraud in measure brings divine punishment, including Hell and standing before the Lord.", "reasons": "ʿIkrima repeatedly swears even his own son, if he measures or weighs, faces the Fire; Ibn ʿUmar warns cheaters stand in sweat, with versions reaching half the ears or the mouth. Al-Fuḍayl says the cheating balance blackens the face. Abū Ṣāliḥ Ḥamdūn tells a holder of scales to recall the scale that will weigh him. ʿAbd Allāh points to 83:6 for accountability. Ibn ʿUmar includes knowingly renting a false measure or employing a cheater; al-Rāzī says even intending fraud is a grave sin."}, {"id": "83:1/q07/p2", "position": "Cheating measures brings failed crops, famine, or drought among five paired communal wrongs and calamities.", "reasons": "Prophetic reports pair broken covenants with enemy domination, unjust judgment with poverty, sexual immorality with death or plague, and withholding zakat with withheld rain. Al-Qurṭubī says al-Bazzār transmits the gist and Mālik gives an Ibn ʿUmar route; Study Quran states no grading. One shorter report pairs only covenants and crops."}, {"id": "83:1/q07/p3", "position": "The warning covers even minute or intended wrongdoing and implies that greater theft is graver.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī reports that proponents of the threat address Muslims: unbelief would already explain the threat and 83:4–5 reminds believers of resurrection. He says intention itself is major sin and favors a threat for any amount without conditioning it on the theft threshold, repentance, or outweighing good deeds. A Bedouin challenges ʿAbd al-Malik to consider seizure of much more Muslim property if slight fraud brings this threat."}, {"id": "83:1/q07/p4", "position": "Fair measurement matters because transactions and reciprocal justice depend on it.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī cites 55:7–9 and 57:25 on the balance and justice. Qatādah tells people to give fairly as they wish to receive; Islāhī sees the trader's protest against being cheated as evidence of innate recognition of justice. Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾ invokes Shuʿayb's ban on corruption in 11:85. Abū Ḥafṣ and Asad extend the reciprocal duty to all social rights."}, {"id": "83:1/q07/p5", "position": "Justice should precede voluntary generosity when measuring.", "reasons": "ʿAlī stopped a saffron seller giving extra and ordered exact due weight first, then any freely chosen surplus; al-Kashshāf says this trains fairness and distinguishes obligation from extra giving. Mālik advises pouring freely until the buyer's measure is full and releasing one's hand without holding back."}, {"id": "83:1/q07/p6", "position": "A measurer should beware the trade's temptation and both measures and scales.", "reasons": "An Arab or Ubayy warns against seeking favors from those dependent on the rims of measures and tongues of scales; al-Aṣmaʿī also ascribes the saying to a Bedouin and perhaps ʿAlī. Ibn ʿAbbās warns Persians that earlier peoples perished through measure and scale, naming them because they use both whereas Mecca weighs and Medina measures."}, {"id": "83:1/q07/p7", "position": "Dishonest gain can return as a terrifying afterlife image.", "reasons": "Mālik ibn Dīnār says a dying neighbor who used two measures saw them become two fiery mountains; striking them together made them appear larger."}, {"id": "83:1/q07/p8", "position": "The warning can be heard in later public worship and market conduct.", "reasons": "Abū Hurayra reports Medina's deputy reciting the surah at dawn and then praying against a trader who bought full but sold short; another report says he heard the verse when the Prophet left Sabāʿ ibn ʿArṭafa in charge during Khaybar."}, {"id": "83:1/q07/p9", "position": "The revelation to David warns against exposing another's private sin.", "reasons": "Tustarī reports God saying people sin privately and repent publicly, although God does not want their wrongdoing exposed."}]}
{"id": "83:1/q08", "question": "How does this opening connect with the preceding surah and the theme of judgment?", "turns_on": "Whether the link is drawn from the preceding surah's judgment and records, from innate moral knowledge, or from God's attributes and nurture.", "positions": [{"id": "83:1/q08/p1", "position": "It develops al-Infiṭār's ending by detailing judgment, the righteous and the wicked.", "reasons": "Al-Jishumī, Biqāʿī and Islāhī say the prior surah ends with resurrection and divergent fates and this surah elaborates them. Al-Rāzī cites 82:19, where all command belongs to God; Abū Ḥayyān says the new opening singles out a contemptible small-gain sin. Biqāʿī says recording every deed in 82:10 and exact weighing in 21:47 make petty fraud a grave offense. The Study Quran says the surah moves from shortchanging to contrasting fates and ends with sinners mocking the Prophet and believers."}, {"id": "83:1/q08/p2", "position": "It argues from human moral awareness of justice to resurrection and God's fair judgment.", "reasons": "Islāhī contrasts al-Infiṭār's argument from bodily creation with this surah's appeal to moral nature: humans love justice, resent being cheated, and expect different treatment for good and evil. Injustice arises when other motives overpower that nature; 75:14–15 is cited for the Qur'anic argument. Verses 1–6 say cheating betrays failure to expect standing before the Lord, and deniers resist accountability."}, {"id": "83:1/q08/p3", "position": "God's nurturing, wisdom, and mercy frame the surah's demand for fair reckoning.", "reasons": "Biqāʿī says the divine nurturer must question and distinguish those He raises; the name al-Taṭfīf signals the theme. He reads the basmala as perfect wisdom and power, universal mercy through creation and guidance, and special mercy for His party. Qushayrī stresses God's beginningless being, majesty, beauty, expected kindness, and rightful decree."}]}

", "question": "Does the opening wayl function as a literal supplication or a declaration of deserved ruin?", "turns_on": "Whether the opening's traditional classification as a curse implies a literal prayer or describes a conventional declaration of deserved ruin.", "positions": [{"id": "83:1/q13/p1", "position": "It is classified as an invocation or curse.", "reasons": "Al-Zarkashī counts al-Muṭaffifīn with al-Humaza and al-Masad among three surahs that open with an invocation or curse; Abū Shāma gives the same classification, as reported by al-Suyūṭī."}, {"id": "83:1/q13/p2", "position": "It is not a literal prayer; it declares that the wrongdoers deserve the customary cry of ruin.", "reasons": "Sībawayh says a literal prayer would sound ugly and explains it as deserved language of ruin and destruction; al-Suyūṭī likewise says the repeated woe is the phrase Arabs use for those headed for ruin."}]}
{"id": "83:2/q01", "question": "How does the relative clause beginning الذين relate to the condemned defrauders?", "turns_on": "Whether الذين qualifies المطففين in the genitive or is set in the accusative for condemnation; the clause may define the group or describe its conduct.", "positions": [{"id": "83:2/q01/p1", "position": "It is a genitive adjective identifying the defrauders by their conduct.", "reasons": "Al-Naḥḥās gives the genitive adjectival analysis; al-Ālūsī says the clause can define which defrauders are intended; al-Būrsawī says it explains how they defraud and merit condemnation."}, {"id": "83:2/q01/p2", "position": "It describes the defrauders' characteristic conduct.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī offers description as an alternative to defining the class; al-Būrsawī connects their taking in full and more with their condemnation."}, {"id": "83:2/q01/p3", "position": "It is accusative by way of condemnation.", "reasons": "Al-Naḥḥās offers this parsing and says it better suits the verse than the genitive adjective."}]}
{"id": "83:2/q02", "question": "What does اكتالوا mean here?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "83:2/q02/p1", "position": "They take or buy goods by measure from other people.", "reasons": "Al-Wāḥidī and al-Būrsawī compare iktiyāl, taking by measure, with ittizān, taking by weight. {"id": "83:2/q03", "question": "What does على الناس mean and what does على attach to?", "turns_on": "Whether على simply substitutes for من, conveys an owed claim or harm and superiority, or belongs syntactically to يستوفون; sources also differ over whether the two prepositional constructions are synonymous.", "positions": [{"id": "83:2/q03/p1", "position": "It attaches to اكتالوا and means taking measure from people; على can stand for من here.", "reasons": "Al-Farrāʾ and those reporting him ground the alternation in collecting what someone owes. Ibn Qutayba adduces Ṣakhr al-Ghayy's على أقطارها glossed من أقطارها. Al-Ṭabarī, al-Thaʿlabī, al-Māwardī, al-Baghawī and others give the from-people gloss. Al-Samīn calls this analysis clearer; Abū Ḥayyān prefers attaching the phrase directly to اكتالوا. Al-Farrāʾ's two descriptions distinguish an amount owed from the act of receiving it; al-Samīn reports a reversed formulation. Al-Ālūsī notes objections that ordinary purchases need no prior debt, then suggests debts acquired in trade as the usual case. Al-Zarkashī cites 5:107 and 19:71 as further examples of على conveying a from-among or from sense, alongside measuring from people here."}, {"id": "83:2/q03/p2", "position": "على implies that taking from people burdens, harms, or dominates them.", "reasons": "Al-Zamakhsharī, al-Rāzī, al-Nasafī, Abū Ḥayyān and al-Samīn connect the choice of على over من with injury and oppression. Al-Bayḍāwī allows either a due owed or oppressive taking. Al-Biqāʿī sees superiority over customers and exploitation of anyone, especially the weak. Al-Būrsawī, al-Ālūsī, Elmalılı and al-Sāmarrāʾī describe domination or seizure; al-Ālūsī cites compacting and shaking the measure as means of harm. Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī likewise reads harm in على. Al-Sāmarrāʾī contrasts neutral اكتال منه, which need not imply unfair taking, with اكتال عليه, which signals domination and makes على more forceful than من."}, {"id": "83:2/q03/p3", "position": "على attaches to يستوفون; its fronting emphasizes that they take fully from others in particular.", "reasons": "Al-Zamakhsharī proposes this attachment and fronting; al-Nasafī and Abū Ḥayyān transmit it. Al-Samīn calls it good. Al-Ālūsī reports a criticism that taking fully from oneself is an implausible contrast, and a defense that the contrast is harm to others rather than themselves; he remains unconvinced."}, {"id": "83:2/q03/p4", "position": "على here means مع, 'with the people' or 'at the people.'", "reasons": "Ibn Qutayba explicitly glosses it مع الناس; al-Qurṭubī reports al-Ṭabarī's 'at' or 'with' gloss."}, {"id": "83:2/q03/p5", "position": "اكتال عليه expresses taking what is owed, whereas اكتال منه expresses receiving full measure; the constructions are distinct.", "reasons": "Al-Naḥḥās explicitly denies synonymy. Al-Farrāʾ as reported by several sources distinguishes taking what is due from receiving the full measure, although the reports differ in which expression receives which gloss."}]}
{"id": "83:2/q04", "question": "How can the verb take على if its ordinary complement is من?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "83:2/q04/p1", "position": "The verb carries an implied sense of imposing or bearing down on others, which licenses على.", "reasons": "Al-Zamakhsharī as quoted in al-Burhān supplies تحاملوا. Al-Burhān says a verb's preposition can follow an implied meaning; its examples construe الرفث as الإفضاء in 4:187 and drinking by a spring as being quenched by it in 76:6. Al-Qāḍī Abū Bakr gives a broader account of تضمين as unstated meaning supplied by form or semantic necessity: معلوم entails an عالم, and ضارب a مضروب; he calls it concise expression and illustrates it with the basmala's implied instruction to begin acts in God's name for reverence or blessing."}]}
{"id": "83:2/q05", "question": "Why is measuring, but not weighing, named for what they take from others?", "turns_on": "Whether measurement stands for both trading modes, reflects opportunities for fraud, or describes the actual goods and practices of the first traders.", "positions": [{"id": "83:2/q05/p1", "position": "Mentioning measurement suffices to imply weighing in trade.", "reasons": "Al-Zajjāj says buying and selling use both measured and weighed goods, so either term can indicate the other; al-Wāḥidī, Ibn al-Jawzī and al-Ṭabrisī transmit or accept this. Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī objects that the reasoning applies equally to omitting measure and is arbitrary."}, {"id": "83:2/q05/p2", "position": "Buying by measure offered more scope than buying by weight to take deliberate extra fullness.", "reasons": "Al-Biqāʿī says selling short is possible by either measure or weight, while acquiring extra fullness is easier by measure."}, {"id": "83:2/q05/p3", "position": "The buyers usually purchased produce by measure and paid with weighed coin.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr uses the different treatment of buying and selling to identify the fraud as a merchants' practice."}, {"id": "83:2/q05/p4", "position": "Dealers commonly bought grain in bulk and resold smaller measured portions.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī records this proposed explanation and calls it weak."}, {"id": "83:2/q05/p5", "position": "The original cheaters bought only by measure but sold by both measure and weight.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī records this explanation and rejects it as unsupported."}]}
{"id": "83:2/q06", "question": "What does يستوفون say they take?", "turns_on": "Whether taking in full names exact receipt, whose blame arises from the contrasting shortfall, or also names taking excess through force and manipulation.", "positions": [{"id": "83:2/q06/p1", "position": "They insist on receiving the full amount due to themselves when buying.", "reasons": "Al-Zajjāj extends the demand to weight; al-Wāḥidī's commentators, al-Ṭabrisī, al-Baghawī's al-Zajjāj, Ibn al-Jawzī's al-Zajjāj, Abū Ḥayyān, al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī and Asad contrast this with shorting others. Al-Ālūsī reports the objection that full receipt is ordinarily proper, then answers that the unequal paired conduct makes it blameworthy."}, {"id": "83:2/q06/p2", "position": "They take more than their right or use tricks to obtain an abundant measure.", "reasons": "Al-Māwardī says the cheater takes more than owed; al-Qurṭubī reports al-Zajjāj's extra-for-self gloss. {"id": "83:2/q08", "question": "What is the actual pattern of trade described by this verse and its next clause?", "turns_on": "Whether the notes state the general unequal transaction or report the specific device of two sets of measures and scales.", "positions": [{"id": "83:2/q08/p1", "position": "The traders require full measure or weight when receiving goods but give less when supplying others.", "reasons": "Al-Wāḥidī's commentators, al-Ṭabrisī, Ibn al-Jawzī's al-Zajjāj, al-Qurṭubī's al-Zajjāj, Abū Ḥayyān, al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī and Asad state the two-sided pattern. {"id": "83:2/q09", "question": "What is the small shortfall called taṭfīf that the clause exemplifies?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "83:2/q09/p1", "position": "Taṭfīf is reducing someone's proper measure or weight by a slight, often inconspicuous amount.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī, al-Jishumī and Abū Ḥayyān derive it from something tiny or scant. {"id": "83:2/q10", "question": "What moral wrong and wider lesson does the trading contrast expose?", "turns_on": "How far the unequal transaction is generalized: reciprocal commercial justice, all social rights, or evidence of moral nature and final judgment.", "positions": [{"id": "83:2/q10/p1", "position": "It exposes selfish inconsistency: demanding one's own rights while denying others equal rights.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī treats both verses as one violation of balanced reciprocal claims that corrupts society. Iṣlāḥī says the trader's protest when cheated reveals an innate recognition of justice, overridden by selfishness when he cheats others; he compares thieves, murderers and adulterers who would reject like harm to their own households. Al-Jishumī's general maxim denies superiority except by piety."}, {"id": "83:2/q10/p2", "position": "The warning extends to every practical and moral social relation involving rights and obligations.", "reasons": "Asad explicitly extends the measure metaphor beyond commerce to each person's rights, obligations and possessions; al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī calls reciprocal rights the basis of a balanced society."}, {"id": "83:2/q10/p3", "position": "Innate recognition of justice points to resurrection and divine judgment, which wrongdoers wish to evade.", "reasons": "Iṣlāḥī reasons that the human moral nature distinguishes just and unjust and thus expects different treatment from God. He says motives can overpower that nature without erasing knowledge of right and wrong, connects the reasoning to 75:14–15, and says the traders' conduct shows no expectation of standing before their Lord."}]}
{"id": "83:2/q11", "question": "What inward reading is given to the cheaters' taking of full measure?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "83:2/q11/p1", "position": "They cheat the true scale of justice by exaggerating their own intellectual and practical virtues before others.", "reasons": "Al-Qāshānī extends measurement to character and deeds and attributes their inflated self-assessment to vanity and pride."}]}
{"id": "83:2/q12", "question": "What reports illustrate the warning about fraudulent measure?", "turns_on": "These are distinct transmitted warnings and examples, with different speakers and consequences.", "positions": [{"id": "83:2/q12/p1", "position": "A Prophetic warning links short measure to drought among five offenses and corresponding calamities.", "reasons": "Al-Qurṭubī reports Ibn ʿAbbās's account: broken covenants bring enemies, rejecting God's law poverty, immorality plague, short measure drought, and withholding alms loss of rain; he says al-Bazzār transmits its gist and Mālik also reports it from Ibn ʿUmar."}, {"id": "83:2/q12/p2", "position": "ʿIkrima warned that every measurer and weigher faces the Fire because none gives exactly what he demands.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī reports ʿIkrima's oath and reason; al-Qurṭubī adds that he did not exempt his son when asked."}, {"id": "83:2/q12/p3", "position": "A trader with two measures saw them become mountains of fire at death.", "reasons": "Al-Qurṭubī reports Mālik ibn Dīnār's account of a dying neighbor who had used two measures, which struck together in his vision."}, {"id": "83:2/q12/p4", "position": "ʿAlī required an accurate weight before any voluntary excess.", "reasons": "Al-Qurṭubī reports ʿAbd Khayr saying ʿAlī overturned a scale giving excess saffron and ordered exact weight first. He also transmits al-Aṣmaʿī's Bedouin saying that manliness is not in measure rims or scale tongues, also attributed to ʿAlī."}, {"id": "83:2/q12/p5", "position": "Ibn ʿUmar warned that short-measurers will stand in sweat up to half their ears.", "reasons": "Al-Qurṭubī transmits this through Nāfiʿ."}, {"id": "83:2/q12/p6", "position": "A recitation of this sura at dawn prompted a prayer against a trader who bought full but sold short.", "reasons": "Al-Qurṭubī reports Abū Hurayra's account of Medina's deputy reciting the sura and the ensuing prayer."}, {"id": "83:2/q12/p7", "position": "ʿAbd Allāh said Medina's people should fulfill measures because God warned against fraud and judgment.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī reports his reply after being told Medina's people fulfill measures, invoking 83:1 and 83:6."}]}
{"id": "83:2/q13", "question": "What setting or occasion of revelation is given for the warning?", "turns_on": "Whether the reports locate the occasion among the Anṣār, a wider early Medinan audience, or earlier market practice; Iṣlāḥī questions the Anṣār attribution.", "positions": [{"id": "83:2/q13/p1", "position": "Dishonest measuring among the Anṣār in Medina occasioned the verse.", "reasons": "Iṣlāḥī reports this from exegetes but challenges it: he treats the sura as Meccan and finds dishonest trade at least as plausible among Meccan traders as among the agricultural Anṣār."}, {"id": "83:2/q13/p2", "position": "The opening warning addressed widespread short measure in early Medina, including its polytheists and those of Mecca.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr says the passage warns Muslims against the practice and condemns the polytheists of both cities."}, {"id": "83:2/q13/p3", "position": "The fraud was practiced in a pre-Islamic market using two sets of measures and scales.", "reasons": "Muqātil reports buyers taking extra and sellers giving short by switching measures and scales."}]}
{"id": "83:2/q14", "question": "Where and when was this opening revealed?", "turns_on": "The Medinan arrival traditions and contextual inference versus Iṣlāḥī's Meccan dating and criticism of the Anṣār report.", "positions": [{"id": "83:2/q14/p1", "position": "At least the first four verses were revealed shortly after the Prophet arrived in Medina.", "reasons": "Asad cites authentic traditions in al-Ṭabarī, al-Baghawī and Ibn Kathīr; al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī says the opening context points to Medina."}, {"id": "83:2/q14/p2", "position": "The sura is Meccan.", "reasons": "Iṣlāḥī uses its Meccan setting to challenge the report assigning the occasion to dishonest measuring among the Anṣār; he notes Meccan traders were at least as likely to practice it."}]}
{"id": "83:2/q15", "question": "How does this warning connect to its surrounding verses and to al-Infiṭār?", "turns_on": "The immediate sequence develops the judgment warning, while the inter-sura account compares two ways of arguing for that judgment.", "positions": [{"id": "83:2/q15/p1", "position": "The contrast in verses 1–6 leads from dishonest measure to resurrection and standing for judgment.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī says the opening warns of the Great Day before the sura describes wicked and righteous fates. Iṣlāḥī says the cheaters act as though they will not stand before their Lord; al-Ṭabarī's report of ʿAbd Allāh invokes 83:1 and 83:6 together."}, {"id": "83:2/q15/p2", "position": "The sura supplements al-Infiṭār by developing its division of righteous and defiant people through an argument from moral nature.", "reasons": "Iṣlāḥī says al-Infiṭār reasons from God's attributes in the human body, while this sura reasons from the human recognition of justice and evil; the dishonest trader who objects to being cheated makes that recognition visible."}]}
